query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Tailored thermo‐mechanical processing that refines the eutectic lamellar microstructure of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 will enhance both strength and ductility simultaneously relative to the as‐cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a relatively coarse lamellar (dual-phase) microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermo‐mechanical processing route—such as a defined degree of severe cold-rolling followed by an optimized annealing treatment—to modify and refine the existing lamellar structure.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at room temperature under tensile loading; processing parameters (rolling reduction and annealing temperature/time) selected to preserve the inherent eutectic lamellar architecture while refining grain size.
generation.structural_mediator: A heterogeneous, ultrafine-grained duplex lamellar microstructure in which the hard phase (e.g., BCC/B2) and soft phase (e.g., FCC) are spatially adjusted to induce a two-hierarchical constraint effect.
generation.mechanism: The processing creates a finer and more heterogeneous lamellar structure that enables dual benefits: the hard ultrafine regions contribute to increased strength, while preserved or slightly modulated soft lamellae provide enhanced ductility through effective strain accommodation and microcrack arresting.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast condition (e.g., ~944 MPa strength and ~25% ductility), the processed alloy is expected to exhibit a notable increase in tensile strength (on the order of a 20–30% improvement) along with maintained or slightly enhanced ductility.
generation.baseline: Mechanical performance of as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA as reported in earlier studies.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated only under processing conditions that maintain the eutectic lamellar structure. Excessive grain refinement or processing conditions that disrupt the lamellae could degrade the desired balance; the effect is assumed to hold primarily at room temperature and under quasi-static load conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While literature supports the strategy through similar interventions, the exact magnitude of improvements and the optimal processing window remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple batches of AlCoCrFeNi2.1. One batch remains as-cast (baseline) while others are processed via different degrees of cold-rolling followed by annealing at varied temperatures/times designed to refine the lamellar structure without complete dissolution. Characterize the microstructure (using SEM/TEM) to verify the dual-scale lamellar architecture. Conduct tensile tests at room temperature to measure tensile strength and ductility.
measurements: Grain size and lamellar spacing (via microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If none of the thermomechanical processing conditions produce a statistically significant simultaneous increase (e.g., at least 20% higher strength) along with an unchanged or improved ductility relative to the as-cast alloy, or if the refined heterogeneous lamellar microstructure is not confirmed, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. To tackle the aforementioned problems, eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [] were proposed. On the one hand, EHEAs should have the general character of traditional eutectic alloys. In this sense, EHEAs should have better fluidity and thus better castability and less casting defects [,]. On the other hand, EHEAs as one kind of in-situ composites with lamellar or rod-like eutectic microstructures might reach the balance between strength and ductility via mixing the soft FCC phase with the hard BCC phase or intermetallic compound [,,,,,,,,]. Some EHEAs indeed have outstanding properties. Lu et al. [] reported the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with simultaneous high strength (944 MPa) and good ductility (25.6%). The excellent mechanical properties do not depend significantly on derivation of eutectic compositions []. After cold-rolling and annealing, its strength reached up to 1.2 GPa and its elongation could remain at about 12% []. After cryo-rolling and annealing, its strength could reach up to 1.47 GPa while its ductility could even increase to 14% []. He et al.
